chunks: MCU vs ASIC vs FPGA. The question: When do use MCU vs ASIC vs FPGA?
A microcontroller (MCU) runs a program one step at a time on a fixed chip.
An FPGA is a chip whose internal wiring you configure after it is made, so it becomes custom hardware that does many things at once.
An ASIC is a chip designed and manufactured for one job and cannot be changed.
The usual rule is to start with the cheapest option that works, an MCU, and move up only when a requirement forces you to.
Think of printing a book. An MCU is a person copying pages by hand: cheap to start and very flexible, but slow. An FPGA is a print shop with rearrangeable type blocks.
You set it up once for your job, then it prints many pages at the same time. An ASIC is a press built for that exact book.
Each copy is the cheapest of all, but building the press costs a fortune, and if you find a typo the press must be rebuilt.
Total cost against volume on log axes. The FPGA is cheaper than the ASIC below about 73,000 units and more expensive above it, because its unit cost is 13 times higher.
The MCU line stays cheapest if the MCU can meet the requirements at all, which is why the first question is feasibility, not cost.
(The MCU and ASIC lines cross at the far right only because I gave both similar placeholder unit costs; it is an artefact, not a design rule.)
MCU: a small chip that runs a stored program, one instruction at a time ("Microcontroller vs microprocessor").
FPGA: a chip you configure after manufacture to form your own digital circuit. ASIC: a chip custom-made for one job, with wiring fixed at the factory.
NRE: the one-time cost to design the chip and set up manufacturing. Parallelism: doing many operations at the same moment.
Break-even: the volume at which two options cost the same in total.
A filter (math that cleans up a signal) must do 64 multiplications for each of 100 million measurements, or samples, per second. That is 6. 4 billion multiplications per second.
A 100 megahertz MCU does one per tick, 100 million per second, which is 64 times too slow. An FPGA with 64 multiplier blocks at 200 megahertz does 12.
8 billion per second, so it fits. That is the whole idea.
"Default to an MCU: it's cheapest, quickest to develop and the most flexible, but it executes sequentially.
Use an FPGA when you need massive parallelism, nanosecond deterministic latency or custom interfaces, with low NRE and reprogrammability but higher unit cost and power.
Use an ASIC only at very high volume with a stable design, since NRE is in the millions and a bug means a respin.
The break-even is NRE plus unit cost times volume, and hybrids like SoC FPGAs are common."
